idea: Shorten the stable–decay schedule from 50% warmdown to a 10% warmdown, initially retaining the existing linear decay and all learning rates.
source: `train.py:445-447, 518-525`; [MiniCPM: Unveiling the Potential of Small Language Models with Scalable Training Strategies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.06395)
why_selected: This is a low-complexity, high-leverage experiment. The current model spends half of its short five-minute run below peak learning rate, potentially sacrificing useful high-rate training.
evidence: The baseline uses no warmup and begins decaying halfway through training. MiniCPM’s WSD experiments reported that a decay stage of about 10% of total tokens was sufficient for their best results, whereas 2.5% was insufficient ([paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.06395)).
hypothesis: With the same seed, 300-second budget, data, and evaluation, `WARMDOWN_RATIO=0.1` will process more updates at the peak learning rate and finish with lower `val_bpb` than `0.5`.
expected_effect: Likely a small-to-moderate decrease in `val_bpb`; this is the highest-priority first experiment.

idea: Halve the optimizer batch from 524,288 to 262,144 tokens while initially retaining the existing learning rates.
why_selected: The current batch requires two accumulated microbatches per update. Halving it removes accumulation and approximately doubles update frequency, which may be valuable in a run lasting only 300 seconds.
evidence: At the current device batch, `TOTAL_BATCH_SIZE=2**19` produces two microsteps per optimizer step; `2**18` produces one. McCandlish et al. found that batches beyond a task-dependent critical size waste computation, and that the critical size varies during training ([paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.06162)).
hypothesis: A fixed-budget run at `TOTAL_BATCH_SIZE=2**18` will obtain enough additional parameter updates to outweigh optimizer-step overhead and will beat the baseline `val_bpb`.
expected_effect: Likely a small-to-moderate decrease in `val_bpb`; monitor total processed tokens because excessive optimizer overhead could instead cause a small increase.

idea: Share one token-derived value-embedding table across all layers currently receiving value residuals, as an SVFormer-inspired variant.
why_selected: Value embeddings are unusually expensive in this small model. Sharing them preserves the value-residual pathway while substantially reducing dense embedding parameters and optimizer state.
evidence: The current 8-layer, 512-wide configuration creates four separate 8,192×512 value tables: 16,777,216 parameters. One shared table would save 12,582,912 parameters. The ResFormer paper describes SVFormer, in which layers share the same first-layer value embedding, and reports only a small performance penalty for that more efficient variant ([paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17897)). This proposal is inspired by SVFormer but is not an exact reproduction because the present code uses token lookup tables.
hypothesis: Sharing the value table will improve training throughput and token exposure enough that a 300-second run achieves lower `val_bpb` despite reduced layer-specific capacity.
expected_effect: Potentially a moderate decrease in `val_bpb`; risk is a small increase if independent value tables are providing essential capacity.

idea: Use grouped-query attention with two KV heads for the existing four query heads.
source: `train.py:64-81, 137-141, 469-476`; [GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models from Multi-Head Checkpoints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.13245); [Gemma 2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.00118)
why_selected: The attention implementation already permits fewer KV than query heads. Two KV heads are a conservative midpoint that reduces both K/V projections and the especially large value-embedding tables.
evidence: For the baseline configuration, moving from four to two KV heads removes about 2.10M K/V projection parameters and 8.39M value-embedding parameters. GQA shares K/V heads within query groups and was reported to retain quality close to multi-head attention ([GQA paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.13245)). Gemma 2’s controlled MHA-versus-GQA ablation found few performance changes and selected GQA for its lower parameter count ([Gemma 2 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.00118)).
hypothesis: Two-KV-head GQA will preserve sufficient attention capacity while its lower compute and optimizer cost allow more tokens within 300 seconds, producing lower `val_bpb`.
expected_effect: Likely a small-to-moderate decrease in `val_bpb`; more promising than immediately attempting single-head MQA.

idea: Replace the 4× ReLU² MLP with a parameter-matched SwiGLU MLP, using an intermediate width near 8/3 of the model dimension.
why_selected: The MLP is a major fraction of per-token compute, so its activation and parameter allocation directly affect fixed-budget quality. Parameter matching keeps the comparison meaningful.
evidence: The current MLP uses two matrices with a 4× hidden dimension and a squared ReLU. Shazeer’s controlled Transformer experiments found that SwiGLU and GEGLU produced the best perplexities among the tested standard and gated FFN variants ([paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.05202)). An 8/3-width SwiGLU approximately matches the current MLP’s matrix parameter count because it uses three projections rather than two.
hypothesis: A parameter-matched SwiGLU model trained for the same 300 seconds will learn better token representations and achieve lower `val_bpb` without a material throughput loss.
expected_effect: Likely a small decrease in `val_bpb`; it could be neutral if the extra gating operations reduce wall-clock token throughput.

idea: Reduce only the local `S` attention window from 1,024 to 512 tokens while retaining the `SSSL` pattern and full 2,048-token layers.
why_selected: This directly tests whether the baseline is spending too much of its fixed wall-clock budget on local attention. Full-attention layers remain available for long-range information.
evidence: The current `S` window is half of the 2,048-token context, with a full layer every fourth layer and the final layer forced full. Longformer demonstrates that layered local attention can build contextual representations efficiently when combined with global access ([paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.05150)). Gemma 2 reported only a small validation-perplexity change when reducing its local inference window from 4,096 to 1,024 while retaining global layers ([paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.00118)); training-time behavior still needs direct testing here.
hypothesis: A 512-token local window will increase tokens processed during 300 seconds enough to offset its reduced local receptive field and lower `val_bpb`.
expected_effect: Expected to be neutral to a small decrease in `val_bpb`; reject if throughput barely changes or BPB rises measurably.

idea: Tie the input token embedding and output language-model matrix in a second-wave experiment.
source: `train.py:129-133, 225-227, 241-253, 273, 283`; [Using the Output Embedding to Improve Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/1608.05859)
why_selected: The baseline maintains two independent 8,192×512 vocabulary matrices. Tying them removes 4,194,304 parameters and imposes a potentially useful language-modeling regularizer.
evidence: The input embedding and `lm_head` are currently independent and even use very different learning rates. Press and Wolf found that tying language-model input and output embeddings improved perplexity across their tested neural language models while reducing model size ([paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1608.05859)).
hypothesis: After selecting an appropriate shared-matrix learning rate, weight tying will produce lower fixed-budget `val_bpb` than the untied baseline through better statistical sharing and lower optimizer overhead.
expected_effect: Possibly a small decrease in `val_bpb`, but higher experimental risk because the current embedding and unembedding learning rates differ by 150×.
